newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia warns tourists of travel risk.
newsitem.headline: Colombia warns tourists of travel risk.

text.p: Colombia on Monday advised foreign embassies to issue an urgent warning to tourists and business people about the dangers of travel in this Andean nation.

Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia's public request came less than a week after an Austrian and a German tourist were killed by leftist guerrillas in the northwest of the country a month after they had been kidnapped.

The body of another tourist, a Russian cyclist who had been pedalling his way through Colombia, was found in a shallow grave in the same region just before the weekend. He disappeared a year ago and is also thought to have fallen victim to Marxist rebels.

"It is important that embassies and consulates warn tourists of the difficulties that we may be experiencing in some parts of Colombia," Mejia said during a speech in a forum on human rights and international affairs at Bogota's Javeriana University.

It is somewhat unusual for a government to draw attention to its internal problems in such a public fashion. Usually it would leave travel advice to the discretion of foreign embassies rather than recommend they issue warnings.

In the wake of the murder of Johann Kehrer, of Linz, Austria, in northwest Choco province last Tuesday, Austrian ambassador Franz Irbinger said: "We're always informing our ministers in Austria of the problems and we have an information section for travelers. But people must be aware of the situation and must bear their share of the responsibility."
Kehrer and his German friend Alexander Sheurer were captured and later killed after trekking through the Darien Gap from Panama into Colombia. Two fellow backpackers survived.

A recent travel advisory from the U.S State Department warned: "Violence continues to affect a significant portion of the country. U.S. citizens have been the victims of recent kidnappings and threats ... Colombia is one of the most dangerous countries in the world."
Most embassies impose stringent travel restrictions on their Bogota-based staff and only allow them to venture outside the capital on vital business.
More than 1,400 people were kidnapped in Colombia last year, the highest abduction rate in the world. Half were attributed to leftist guerrillas fighting a long-running war against the state.

Colombia also has the highest murder rate in Latin America with 89.5 killings per 100,000 population, slightly higher than Jamaica and more than four times greater than Brazil, a recent World Bank report stated.
